implementation_notes: The stdlib models the fallible call as a value: `Try { call() }` wraps the outcome in Success or Failure and, as the API documentation notes, only non-fatal exceptions are caught, while combinators such as recover and recoverWith supply default behaviour on failure. The mute is therefore either a discarded Try or an explicit `.recover { case NonFatal(_) => () }` that names the ignored class - NonFatal exists precisely to keep VirtualMachineError, LinkageError and threading control exceptions out of such handlers. Where the mute covers a statement rather than an expression, the classic `try { call() } catch { case NonFatal(_) => () }` form is still the idiomatic realization.
pitfalls: `case _ => ()` instead of `case NonFatal(_)` also swallows fatal errors and control exceptions such as InterruptedException and ControlThrowable, which breaks cancellation and resource safety.

A Try that is constructed and discarded is never inspected: nothing in the type system forces a second look, so the mute must be a statement with the justification beside it rather than a value nobody reads.
Try captures whatever the by-name block throws, so wrapping more than the single call silently widens the mute past the failure that was analysed.
